title: Finishing a Song
intro: A song is finished when someone else can play it and hear it. That means writing it down in a form musicians read, and making a recording, however simple.

blocks.text: A lead sheet is the standard way to write a song: the melody on one staff, the chord symbols above it, the lyrics below, and the form marked with section labels, repeat signs and endings. It is what jazz and pop musicians read (see chord symbols (#/arts/music-theory/chords/extended-and-altered) and Notation (#/arts/music-theory/sound-and-pitch/notation)).

For players who already know the tune, a chord chart is quicker: bars with chord symbols (or Nashville numbers, see Harmony and Progressions (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/harmony-and-progressions)), section labels and any important hits or stops. Guitarists often also write tab for riffs and capo position at the top.

blocks.source:
SONG TITLE            Key: G   Capo: none   Tempo: 92   Feel: straight 8ths

INTRO   | G      | Cadd9  | G      | Cadd9  |
VERSE   | Em     | C      | G      | D      |  x2
CHORUS  | C      | G      | D      | Em     |
        | C      | G      | D      | D      |
BRIDGE  | Am     | Bm     | C      | D7     |

items: Record a scratch track to a click (metronome) first: one instrument and the voice. Everything else is built on it, so the tempo must be steady.

A computer, a USB audio interface, one microphone and free or low-cost software (a digital audio workstation, DAW: GarageBand, free on a Mac; Reaper, inexpensive with a free trial; or Audacity for basic recording) are enough to make a clean demo.

Acoustic guitar: point a small condenser mic at the 12th fret, about 15–30 cm away. Piano: two mics over the hammers, or a digital piano recorded directly. Vocals: about 15 cm from the mic with a pop filter.
Record each instrument on its own track so you can balance them later; leave peaks around −10 to −6 dBFS so nothing clips.
Mix with volume and panning first (piano and guitar placed slightly apart, voice in the middle), then a little EQ to cut low-frequency mud from everything except the bass.
The title appears in the hook, ideally the first or last line of the chorus.
Every section has a reason to exist; cut anything that repeats without adding something.
The melody's high point arrives in the chorus or the bridge.
The arrangement builds: something new enters or drops out at each section.
Someone else can play it from your chart.

blocks.title: Gain staging
blocks.text: Why record with peaks around −10 dBFS rather than as close to 0 dBFS as possible?
solution: 0 dBFS is the digital ceiling: anything above clips (distorts) irreparably. Modern 24-bit recording has so much dynamic range that recording lower costs nothing in noise, and the headroom absorbs unexpectedly loud moments.
blocks.answer: To leave headroom so peaks never clip; 24-bit audio loses nothing by recording lower
